posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring CRO post with three strong ICP prospects engaging — validate the explainability problem from an operator's perspective, position auditability as the real unlock, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is the thing that kills adoption faster than any technical failure. It's not really a trust gap — it's a provenance gap. Finance and risk teams don't need AI to be perfect, they need to be able to retrace every step when someone puts a number in front of a regulator. Curious whether your team found that the ban actually slowed things down, or whether people were quietly routing around the tools anyway?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that the data isn't the issue, the audit trail is
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. It's that when someone asks 'where does this number come from?' and the answer is 'the BI tool,' that's not actually an answer — and finance people know it. Excel feels safer because everyone can trace the formula. Have you tried figuring out exactly which number they stopped trusting first?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs isn't a dashboard, it's a confession that nobody agreed on what mattered. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells you everything — people don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because they've learned the dashboard won't help them make a call. The real problem isn't measurement, it's that most tools are built to impress the person who commissioned them, not the person staring at them at 9am trying to decide something. What made those 5 the ones that survived the cut?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging on a post about BI chaos and data definition problems — validate the core pain around semantic disagreement, add the insight that tooling is downstream of governance, never upstream
posts.draft_comment: The 'three definitions of revenue' thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. The mistake is thinking more access fixes it — you can't democratise data that nobody's agreed on yet. The tool is always downstream of the governance conversation, not upstream of it. Who actually owned the definition problem before the Power BI rollout happened?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the security framing, add the trust/audit trail angle, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right. Most teams treat a hallucinated number as an oops moment — clean it up, move on. But if that number touched a board deck or a compliance report, the damage is already done and there's often no audit trail showing where it came from. The question isn't just 'was the output wrong' — it's 'can you prove how it was generated?'

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: COO at a consulting firm (ICP prospect) is watching this thread — validate the £200k waste pain with a specific observation about who BI tools are actually designed for, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number stings but it's almost always the same story — the tool gets built around the person who can query a database, not the person who needs to make a call on Monday morning. Vendors demo to data teams because data teams are the ones in the room during procurement. The actual end users, the ops lead, the account director, don't see it until it's too late to say anything. Who even signed off on that purchase?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company naming the real root cause (culture, not tools) — validate the diagnosis and add the layer he might be missing about what actually bridges the two
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is real but I'd push back slightly on the framing — culture explains why it happened, but it doesn't fix the three people who now trust different numbers. Someone has to decide which version is true and make that the only version that exists. The hardest part isn't the technology or even the behaviour change, it's that nobody wants to be the person who tells two teams their numbers were wrong. Who owned that conversation after the CFO meeting?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' adoption problem — validate the real barrier (query literacy, not tool quality) and add a sharper framing around why locked-down AI creates shadow behaviour
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all — the dirty secret with most of these tools is that knowing what to ask is half the job, and that's not something a rollout solves. Shadow AI filling the gap makes complete sense too. When the official tool feels like it needs a prompt engineering degree and the unofficial one just answers, people vote with their phones. The question isn't really how do you get adoption up — it's why are the answers so hard to get to in the first place?
